detail:
The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) describes asthma treatment as a plan built with a clinician and adjusted over time, based on age, asthma severity, and response to a given treatment. Most treatment plans in the sources combine long-term control medicines taken daily with a quick-relief inhaler used when symptoms occur, together with monitoring and steps to avoid the triggers that set symptoms off for that person. An asthma action plan is presented as the written guide for day-to-day control and for responding when symptoms worsen.

Medicine classes in the sources include inhaled short-acting beta2-agonists and short-acting anticholinergics for quick relief, and corticosteroids, biologic medicines, leukotriene modifiers, mast cell stabilizers, and inhaled long-acting bronchodilators for long-term control, with immunotherapy described for allergic asthma in some cases. NHLBI notes that severe attacks may be treated in emergency care with medicines given by nebulizer or intravenously, oxygen, or breathing assistance, and that a procedure called bronchial thermoplasty is described only for certain adults whose severe asthma remains uncontrolled despite other treatments.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing asthma and asthma action plans.
sourceName: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
summary: NHLBI outlines asthma treatment as an adjustable plan combining daily long-term control medicines, quick-relief medicines for symptoms, trigger avoidance, and a written action plan, with emergency care and procedures reserved for severe or uncontrolled cases.
takeaways: treatment combines daily control medicines and quick relief
an action plan guides day-to-day care and worsening symptoms
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
title: Asthma: daily control medicines, quick relief, and an action plan
